blocks.en_title: 导读
blocks.src:
> 本导读整理自 Socratopia 网站本书介绍页：https://www.socratopia.app/library/behavioral-economics-en

Most behavioral economics books give you a tour of the cognitive zoo: here's anchoring, here's loss aversion, here's the availability heuristic. When Humans Don't Compute gives you something different — the underlying machinery. You get the value function, the β-δ discounting model, the Fehr-Schmidt inequality-aversion utility function — not as decorative formalism, but as tools that generate testable predictions. When the book tells you that loss aversion explains the disposition effect in financial markets, the endowment effect in mug experiments, and systematic undersaving for retirement, you understand why: the same mechanism, working in three different contexts, produces three different phenomena.

The book is structured around three interlocking narrative threads. Thread A follows a single policy problem — retirement undersaving — across all 22 chapters, from the rational agent's prediction of optimal saving to the complete behavioral toolkit (automatic enrollment, SMarT escalation, target-date fund defaults) that addresses it. Thread B runs a chapter-by-chapter comparison between what standard economics predicts and what humans actually do, building toward a nuanced verdict in Chapter 22: the rational agent model is a useful limiting case, not a description of anyone. Thread C is the one most behavioral economics books skip: it tracks the replication crisis honestly, using ego depletion — a finding cited hundreds of times that essentially vanished under pre-registered replication — as the central case study in how to read behavioral research critically.

By the end, you have a practical framework for evaluating behavioral claims: What was the sample size? Has it been pre-registered? Does the lab effect appear in field settings? What is the implied mechanism, and does that mechanism predict correctly in other domains? That framework is arguably more valuable than any individual finding.

**Target audience**：Economics and business students; policy analysts; MBA students; psychologists interested in economic behavior; readers who want the academic depth behind popular behavioral economics books

**Prerequisites**：Introductory economics (basic supply/demand, utility, expected value) is helpful but not required — key concepts are introduced inline

**Study hours**：90–120 hours (including exercises and reflection)

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: The Rational Agent and Why It Matters
blocks.src:
Imagine you are offered the following choice. Option A: receive 1,000 USD with certainty. Option B: flip a fair coin — heads gives you 2,500 USD, tails gives you nothing. Which do you choose?

Most people pick Option A, even though a quick calculation shows that Option B has a higher expected value (1,250 USD versus 1,000 USD). Now imagine a different scenario: you are told that a medical treatment program will save exactly 200 lives. The alternative program has a one-third chance of saving all 600 people at risk and a two-thirds chance of saving no one. Which program do you recommend?

Again, most people prefer the certain option. Something systematic is going on. The pattern is not random noise — it is the same pattern, appearing reliably, across populations, continents, and decades of experiments. That pattern is the starting point for behavioral economics.

This chapter sets the stage. Before we can understand what behavioral economics discovered, we need to understand what it was reacting against: the rational agent model, also called _homo economicus_ — the idealized decision-maker that standard economics built its theories around. We will see why this model is genuinely powerful, why it generates useful predictions, and why it nonetheless fails in systematic, predictable ways that matter enormously for policy, markets, and everyday life.


### 1.1 The Standard Model: Homo Economicus

Standard economics — the kind taught in introductory textbooks and used in most policy analysis — is built on a highly stylized model of human behavior. The model makes several strong assumptions:

**Assumption 1: Complete and consistent preferences.** The rational agent has well-defined preferences over all possible outcomes. Given any two options, they either prefer one to the other, or they are genuinely indifferent. Their preferences do not change depending on how options are described, who asks, or what time of day it is.

**Assumption 2: Maximization.** The rational agent always chooses the option that best satisfies their preferences, given their constraints (budget, time, information). They do not satisfice — choose "good enough" — they optimize.

**Assumption 3: Beliefs updated by Bayes' rule.** When the rational agent receives new information, they update their beliefs in a mathematically precise way. They do not overreact or underreact to evidence; they incorporate it correctly.

**Assumption 4: Time consistency.** If the rational agent prefers option A to option B when both are delivered in the future, they still prefer A to B when both arrive in the present. Their preferences are stable over time.

Together, these assumptions define a decision-maker that economists call _homo economicus_ — economic man. This creature is not human. No actual person satisfies all four assumptions all the time. Economists know this. The question is not whether the model is realistic but whether it is useful — whether it generates accurate predictions about aggregate behavior even if no individual matches it perfectly.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: The Rational Agent and Why It Matters
blocks.src:
#### Definition: The Rational Agent Model

The rational agent model (also called the standard economic model) describes a decision-maker who (1) has complete and consistent preferences over all possible outcomes, (2) chooses the option that maximizes those preferences given their constraints, (3) updates beliefs using Bayes' rule when new information arrives, and (4) maintains time-consistent preferences — what they prefer today they will still prefer tomorrow.

In plain language: the rational agent always knows what they want, always does the calculation correctly, always chooses the best option for themselves, and never changes their mind for bad reasons.


#### Common Misconception

**Misconception:** The rational agent model assumes that people are purely selfish and only care about money.

**Reality:** The model says nothing about the _content_ of preferences. A rational agent could have strong preferences for fairness, generosity, or the welfare of strangers — all that "rational" requires is that preferences are consistent and choices maximize them. A person who consistently donates 30% of their income to charity is perfectly rational under this definition, as long as their behavior reflects stable underlying preferences. Selfishness and rationality are independent properties: you can be rational and generous, or irrational and selfish.


### 1.2 Why the Model Is Powerful

The rational agent model would not have dominated economics for 70 years if it were useless. It has genuine virtues.

**Virtue 1: Predictive discipline.** A model with specific assumptions makes specific predictions. When the rational agent model predicts that raising the price of cigarettes will reduce cigarette consumption, or that rent controls will create housing shortages, those predictions are often correct. The model's precision is what allows economics to function as a policy science.

**Virtue 2: Disciplining intuition.** Human beings have terrible economic intuitions. People support policies that reduce social welfare because they sound fair; they resist policies that increase social welfare because they sound unfair. The rational agent model forces policy analysis to ask: what are the actual incentives created by this policy, and how will people respond to them? This discipline has saved economies from many well-intentioned disasters.

**Virtue 3: Aggregation properties.** Even if individual people make small mistakes, markets with many participants may aggregate toward rational outcomes. Competitive pressure, learning, and arbitrage can wash out individual irrationality. The rational agent model may be most accurate precisely where it matters most: in large, competitive, high-stakes markets.

**Virtue 4: Falsifiability.** Because it makes precise predictions, the rational agent model can be tested — and has been. Behavioral economics did not reject the rational agent model by assertion; it accumulated experimental evidence showing specific, systematic patterns of deviation from the model's predictions. That is how science is supposed to work.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: The Rational Agent and Why It Matters
blocks.src:
#### Thread B — Rational vs. Human Agent

Standard theory predicts: a person deciding how much to save for retirement will calculate their lifetime income stream, expected consumption needs, and optimal savings rate, and then act accordingly. The savings rate that maximizes lifetime utility under a given discount rate is a well-defined mathematical quantity. Any rational person who does not save this amount is making an error.

Human prediction (spoiler for later chapters): most people procrastinate on retirement enrollment, set contribution rates by anchoring to defaults or round numbers, invest in employer stock far beyond what diversification would recommend, and react to market downturns by selling — doing the opposite of what rational lifetime planning would prescribe. We will trace exactly why throughout this book.


### 1.3 The First Cracks: Allais and Ellsberg

The rational agent model was challenged almost from the moment it was formalized. Two thought experiments — both devised within a few years of the expected utility framework being published — revealed that real people violate its core predictions in ways that are not random errors but systematic patterns.


#### The Allais Paradox

Consider two separate choice problems. In each, you must choose between two options.

**Problem 1:**

* Option A: 1,000,000 USD with certainty
* Option B: an 89% chance of 1,000,000 USD, a 10% chance of 5,000,000 USD, and a 1% chance of nothing

**Problem 2:**

* Option C: an 11% chance of 1,000,000 USD and an 89% chance of nothing
* Option D: a 10% chance of 5,000,000 USD and a 90% chance of nothing

When you work through these choices, you may find yourself strongly preferring A over B in Problem 1 (the certainty of a million dollars is attractive — why risk getting nothing?) and D over C in Problem 2 (the difference between 10% and 11% seems small, so why not go for the bigger prize?). This is the most common pattern of choices. It is also a violation of expected utility theory.

Expected utility theory requires that your choices satisfy the _independence axiom_ : if you prefer lottery X to lottery Y, you should still prefer X to Y when both are mixed with the same third lottery Z at the same probability. The A-over-B and D-over-C pattern violates this axiom. You can verify this algebraically: if you prefer A to B, expected utility theory requires you to prefer C to D, not D to C.

The Allais paradox reveals that people have a specific distortion: they overweight certainty relative to near-certainty. Moving from a 100% chance to an 89% chance feels like a huge loss; moving from 11% to 10% feels small. But mathematically, both represent the same absolute reduction in probability. We will formalize this distortion in Chapter 3 through the probability weighting function.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: The Rational Agent and Why It Matters
blocks.src:
#### The Ellsberg Paradox

Now consider an urn containing 90 balls. You know that exactly 30 balls are red. The remaining 60 balls are either black or yellow, in proportions you do not know.

**Problem 1:**

* Option A: win 100 USD if a ball drawn is red
* Option B: win 100 USD if a ball drawn is black

**Problem 2:**

* Option C: win 100 USD if a ball drawn is red or yellow
* Option D: win 100 USD if a ball drawn is black or yellow

Most people prefer A over B (30 red balls is a known probability; black could be anywhere from 0 to 60) and D over C (D is guaranteed to win with at least 60 balls, while C could be as low as 30 + some yellows). But again, this pattern violates expected utility theory's requirements for consistent probability beliefs.

The Ellsberg paradox reveals _ambiguity aversion_ — people dislike uncertainty about probabilities (not knowing the mix of black and yellow) over and above dislike of risk (not knowing which ball will be drawn). Rational agents in the expected utility framework should not care about this distinction; they should assign subjective probabilities to ambiguous events and behave consistently. People do not.


#### Definition: Risk vs. Ambiguity

**Risk** refers to situations where probabilities are known or calculable (like a fair coin flip or a known lottery). **Ambiguity** (also called _Knightian uncertainty_) refers to situations where probabilities themselves are unknown — you face uncertainty about your uncertainty. The Ellsberg paradox shows that people treat these two situations differently, with systematic preference for known-probability gambles over unknown-probability ones.


### 1.4 What Behavioral Economics Is (and Is Not)

The Allais and Ellsberg paradoxes are not just philosophical curiosities. They motivated a research program — behavioral economics — that has accumulated over 50 years of experimental evidence showing that real human decision-making departs from the rational agent model in systematic ways.


#### Definition: Behavioral Economics

Behavioral economics is the study of how psychological, social, and emotional factors influence the economic decisions of individuals and institutions. It combines insights from psychology and economics to build more accurate models of human behavior, with the goal of improving both predictions and policy.

The word "behavioral" signals a commitment to empirical evidence about actual behavior, not assumptions about idealized behavior.

Behavioral economics is often described as a collection of biases — "people anchor too much," "people are loss averse," "people procrastinate." This description is partly accurate but misleading. The deeper goal is not to catalog human flaws but to build better models. A list of biases with no underlying theory is not science; it is trivia. The best behavioral economics research identifies the mechanisms — the systematic patterns in psychology that produce the deviations — and uses those mechanisms to generate new predictions.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: The Rational Agent and Why It Matters
blocks.src:
#### Thread C — The Replication Challenge

Science is not a collection of facts — it is a process. A finding published in a journal is a claim, not a truth. Claims require replication: independent researchers, with different samples, in different contexts, obtaining similar results. Behavioral economics has a mixed replication record. Some findings — prospect theory's basic predictions, the Allais paradox, the ultimatum game results — have replicated robustly across cultures and decades. Others — certain priming effects, ego depletion — have struggled badly when subjected to large-scale pre-registered replications.

Throughout this book, we will track which findings are solid and which are contested. This is not an attack on behavioral economics; it is the appropriate epistemological stance toward any empirical science. The reader who finishes this book should be able to look at a new behavioral finding and ask the right questions: How large was the sample? Has this been replicated? In what populations? Does the lab effect appear in real-world field settings?


### 1.5 The Structure of This Book

This book follows a three-part logic.

**Part I: The Rational Agent and Its Discontents** (Chapters 1–3) builds the standard model properly, then introduces prospect theory as the first comprehensive behavioral alternative.

**Part II: The Behavioral Toolkit** (Chapters 4–14) surveys the major behavioral findings — framing, heuristics, time preferences, social preferences, self-control — and their applications to markets and finance. Each chapter follows the format: what does the rational agent predict? → what do people actually do? → why the gap?

**Part III: Policy and Frontiers** (Chapters 15–22) examines what behavioral economics implies for policy (nudge theory), how it applies in global development contexts, and how its core claims are challenged by the ecological rationality school. Chapter 22 synthesizes: what has behavioral economics actually established, and where does the field go from here?


### 1.6 Exercises

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: The Rational Agent and Why It Matters
blocks.src:
#### Concept Check

**Q1.** The rational agent model assumes four things about decision-makers. List and briefly explain each assumption.

**Answer:** The four assumptions are: (1) _Complete and consistent preferences_ : the agent can rank any pair of outcomes and does so consistently — if they prefer A to B and B to C, they prefer A to C. (2) _Maximization_ : the agent always chooses the option that best satisfies their preferences given constraints; they do not settle for "good enough." (3) _Bayesian belief updating_ : when new information arrives, the agent revises their probabilistic beliefs in the mathematically correct way, neither over- nor under-reacting. (4) _Time consistency_ : preferences are stable over time — what the agent prefers today about future outcomes, they will still prefer when the future arrives.

**Q2.** A student argues: "The rational agent model assumes people are greedy and self-interested. Behavioral economics is better because it allows for altruism." Is this criticism valid? Explain.

**Answer:** No, this is a misconception (the exact one flagged in Section 1.1). The rational agent model makes no claim about the _content_ of preferences. A person who cares deeply about others and behaves consistently with those preferences is perfectly rational. The model requires _consistency_ and _optimization_ , not any particular set of values. Behavioral economics challenges the consistency and optimization assumptions — not the content of preferences. Both rational and behavioral models can accommodate altruism.

**Q3.** Explain the Allais paradox. What axiom of expected utility theory does the most common pattern of choices violate?

**Answer:** The Allais paradox presents two choice problems. In Problem 1, most people prefer A (certain 1M USD) over B (89% chance of 1M USD, 10% chance of 5M USD, 1% chance of nothing). In Problem 2, most people prefer D (10% chance of 5M USD, 90% chance of nothing) over C (11% chance of 1M USD, 89% chance of nothing). This A-over-B and D-over-C pattern violates the _independence axiom_ of expected utility theory, which requires that if you prefer lottery X to lottery Y, you still prefer X to Y when both are mixed with the same third lottery at the same probability. People exhibit a "certainty effect" — they overweight the certain outcome in Problem 1 relative to a merely probable outcome, creating an inconsistency when probabilities are reduced proportionally in Problem 2.

**Q4.** What is the difference between risk and ambiguity? Which does the Ellsberg paradox reveal?

**Answer:** _Risk_ refers to situations with known probabilities (e.g., a fair coin flip). _Ambiguity_ (Knightian uncertainty) refers to situations where the probabilities themselves are unknown. In the Ellsberg urn, you know there are 30 red balls but don't know the black-yellow split. The paradox reveals _ambiguity aversion_ : most people prefer bets on known-probability events (red) even when the logical structure of the problem implies their choices are inconsistent. This shows people treat risk and ambiguity differently — a violation of expected utility theory's requirement for consistent subjective probabilities.

**Q5.** In what sense is the rational agent model "useful" even if no actual person satisfies all its assumptions?

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: The Rational Agent and Why It Matters
blocks.src: **Answer:** A model need not be descriptively accurate at the individual level to generate useful aggregate predictions. Several mechanisms can produce rational-looking outcomes even with individually irrational agents: (1) competitive markets reward and select for more rational behavior, punishing consistent errors; (2) aggregation can average out individual errors; (3) arbitrage by sophisticated actors can eliminate mispricing caused by less rational investors. Moreover, the model provides a disciplined benchmark — by specifying precisely what a rational person would do, it makes deviations visible and measurable. Behavioral economics could not have developed without the rational agent model as a clear foil.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: The Rational Agent and Why It Matters
blocks.src:
#### Application Problems

**Q1.** A friend tells you: "I always choose the safe option when the stakes are high, but I like to gamble for fun when the amounts are small." Is this behavior consistent with the rational agent model? What might explain it?

Hint

Think about whether the utility function can accommodate varying risk preferences at different wealth levels, and whether "stakes" in the rational model refers to absolute amounts or some other measure.

**Answer:** This behavior is potentially consistent with the rational agent model. A utility function that is concave (risk averse) in the region of large wealth changes but relatively linear (near-risk neutral) in the region of small gambles can rationalize preferring safe options for high-stakes decisions while tolerating gambles for low-stakes entertainment. Additionally, a rational person might legitimately derive entertainment utility from gambling — the "fun" is part of the payoff, not just the money. The rational model does not predict uniform risk aversion; it only requires that the utility function be consistent. Where behavioral economics would push back: if the same _pattern_ of choices cannot be rationalized by any consistent utility function, that is when we have a genuine anomaly.

**Q2.** The Allais paradox involves reducing probabilities proportionally from Problem 1 to Problem 2. Construct a small numerical example using three prizes (say, 0 USD, 1 USD, and 4 USD) and three probabilities, showing that a preference for A over B in one problem, combined with a preference for D over C in the other, violates the independence axiom.

Hint

The independence axiom says: if A is preferred to B, then for any lottery Z and any probability p, the mixed lottery (A with probability p, Z with probability 1-p) is preferred to (B with probability p, Z with probability 1-p). Try constructing your two problems so that one is a mixing of the other with a fixed third lottery.

**Answer:** Let the three prizes be 0 USD, 1 USD, and 4 USD. Consider:

* Lottery A: 1 USD with certainty (probability 1)
* Lottery B: 4 USD with probability 0.8, 0 USD with probability 0.2
* Lottery Z: 0 USD with certainty

Now construct Problem 1 by mixing A and B each with Z at probability 0.5:

* Problem 1, Option C: (A at 0.5) + (Z at 0.5) = 1 USD with prob 0.5, 0 USD with prob 0.5
* Problem 1, Option D: (B at 0.5) + (Z at 0.5) = 4 USD with prob 0.4, 0 USD with prob 0.6

Independence axiom says: if you prefer A to B, you must prefer C to D. But many people, seeing Problem 1 in isolation, prefer D over C (40% chance of 4 USD looks attractive compared to 50% chance of 1 USD). If those same people would prefer A to B in isolation (the certain 1 USD beats the risky 4 USD / 0 USD gamble), they have violated independence. The Allais paradox is exactly this structure scaled up to realistic dollar amounts.

**Q3.** A regulatory body is deciding whether to require nutritional labeling on restaurant menus. A staff economist argues: "Under the rational agent model, labels shouldn't affect behavior — people already know roughly how many calories their food contains, and if they didn't care, they'd have found out." A behavioral economist disagrees. Construct the behavioral economist's argument, using at least two concepts from this chapter.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: The Rational Agent and Why It Matters
blocks.src: **Answer:** The behavioral economist would challenge the claim that people "already know" or have optimally acquired information. First, _ambiguity_ : people may face genuine uncertainty (ambiguity, not just risk) about caloric content, and the certainty provided by a label reduces this ambiguity in a way that changes choices — even if the expected caloric content is unchanged. Second, _salience_ : the rational agent model assumes all relevant information is processed equally, but real people are influenced by how prominently information is presented. A calorie count prominently displayed at the point of choice may shift behavior even when the same information in a food database would not — this is a failure of the rational model's assumption that information processing is cost-free and complete. Third, the rational model assumes people already know what they "want" to eat in light of health goals; behavioral evidence suggests people have inconsistent preferences between a cool moment (wanting to be healthy) and the moment of temptation (wanting the burger). Labels may activate the more reflective preference.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: The Rational Agent and Why It Matters
blocks.src:
#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** Some economists argue that behavioral economics is "just applied psychology" and doesn't need to be a separate field within economics. Others argue that economics needed behavioral corrections badly and behavioral economics is rightly changing the field. What would constitute evidence that behavioral economics has genuinely contributed something that psychology alone could not have provided?

**Discussion:** Behavioral economics' distinctive contribution is not the psychological facts themselves (which psychologists discovered) but the economic machinery applied to them. Economists bring three things psychologists typically do not: (1) _welfare analysis_ — the ability to say whether a behavioral pattern makes people better or worse off in a meaningful sense; (2) _equilibrium reasoning_ — asking not just how individuals behave but how markets and institutions emerge when many such individuals interact; (3) _mechanism design_ — using knowledge of behavioral patterns to construct incentive structures that steer behavior toward better outcomes (like the SMarT program we will encounter in Chapter 16). A pure psychology of heuristics and biases tells you that people are present-biased; behavioral economics tells you how to design a retirement plan that accounts for present bias and produces better retirement outcomes. The latter requires both the psychological insight and the economic toolkit.

**Q2.** The rational agent model has been challenged empirically for decades, yet it remains the foundation of most mainstream economics textbooks and policy analysis. Why might a model persist even after substantial evidence against it? What does this tell us about how science works in practice?

**Discussion:** Several factors explain the persistence of a challenged model. First, _replacement problem_ : a model is not abandoned until there is a better model to replace it. Behavioral economics offers many documented deviations from rationality but has been slower to produce a single unified alternative with the rational model's tractability and generality. Second, _domain dependence_ : the rational model may be more accurate in some domains (competitive financial markets, repeated high-stakes decisions) than others (one-time medical choices, retirement planning), so abandonment feels premature. Third, _tractability_ : the rational model generates closed-form solutions; behavioral models often do not. Applied economists resist switching to models that cannot produce clean policy prescriptions. Fourth, _sociological factors_ : paradigms persist partly because trained economists are invested in the existing framework and teaching infrastructure is sticky. This does not mean the rational model is wrong to persist — it may genuinely be the best available benchmark in many contexts. It does mean that science in social domains moves more slowly than pure experimental findings might suggest, and that the accumulation of anomalies alone is rarely sufficient to displace a paradigm.

**Q3.** Behavioral economics assumes that there is a "right" answer to decision problems — that the Allais paradox choices are _violations_ of rationality, not just different but valid preferences. But is this assumption defensible? Could someone argue that preferring certainty is not a bias but a perfectly legitimate preference?

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: The Rational Agent and Why It Matters
blocks.src:
**Discussion:** This is one of the deepest methodological debates in behavioral economics. The critique goes: expected utility theory is a _normative_ theory (how people _should_ choose) as well as a descriptive one. When we call Allais paradox choices "irrational," we are applying a normative standard. But why should the independence axiom be normatively compelling? Some philosophers of decision theory argue that it is not — that preferring certainty for its own sake is a legitimate value that a consistent person could hold, and that calling this a "bias" smuggles in a normative view about how people ought to value certainty. Defenders of the behavioral program respond that: (1) when people are shown the logical structure of the Allais paradox — that their choices imply a formal inconsistency — many report wanting to revise their choices, suggesting the independence axiom does represent something they endorse on reflection; and (2) the patterns observed in the Allais paradox also appear in domains where they clearly cause harm (like people buying lottery tickets instead of insurance), so the normative force of calling them errors is supported by the welfare consequences. The tension between descriptive findings and normative standards remains live in the field.


### Chapter Summary

This chapter introduced the rational agent model — the foundation of standard economics — and the opening challenges to it. The rational agent has complete and consistent preferences, maximizes utility, updates beliefs correctly, and maintains time-consistent preferences. This model is useful precisely because it is precise: it generates falsifiable predictions and provides a disciplined benchmark for policy analysis.

The Allais and Ellsberg paradoxes showed that real people systematically violate the model's core axioms. The Allais paradox reveals a certainty effect — overweighting of certain outcomes relative to probable ones. The Ellsberg paradox reveals ambiguity aversion — dislike of unknown probabilities beyond the dislike of known risk. These patterns are not random errors but systematic deviations that motivate an alternative research program.

Behavioral economics is that research program. It combines psychological insights with economic tools to build more accurate models of actual behavior. Its ambition is not merely to document deviations but to understand their mechanisms and use that understanding to improve predictions and policy.

As we move through this book, we will track three running themes: the comparison between rational-agent predictions and human behavior (Thread B), the behavioral story of retirement savings as a policy domain where all these insights converge (Thread A), and the epistemological question of which behavioral findings are truly robust and which require more scrutiny (Thread C). Chapter 2 builds the expected utility framework formally before Chapter 3 dismantles and rebuilds it through prospect theory.

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: Expected Utility Theory — The Benchmark
blocks.src:
In Chapter 1, we met the rational agent — a decision-maker with consistent preferences who always maximizes utility and updates beliefs correctly. That description is abstract. This chapter makes it concrete.

What does it actually mean to maximize utility when outcomes are uncertain? When you choose between a sure thing and a gamble, what formula governs a rational agent's choice? The answer, developed by John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern in the 1940s, is _expected utility theory_ — the cornerstone of economic decision theory under uncertainty and the benchmark that behavioral economics has spent decades interrogating.

We build the framework here carefully, because you cannot appreciate where behavioral economics departs from rationality if you do not first understand what rational choice looks like in a precise setting.


### 2.1 From Expected Value to Expected Utility

The most natural theory of choice under uncertainty is to maximize expected value: choose the option with the highest probability-weighted average monetary payoff. If a gamble pays 100 USD with probability 0.5 and 0 USD with probability 0.5, its expected value is 0.5 \times 100 + 0.5 \times 0 = 50 USD.

Expected value theory has an obvious prediction: a person should always prefer a gamble with a higher expected value to one with a lower expected value, regardless of risk. A rational expected-value maximizer would prefer any gamble with expected value 51 USD to a certain 50 USD.

This prediction is badly wrong. Most people, faced with a choice between 50 USD certain and a 50/50 gamble for 0 USD or 100 USD, prefer the certain 50 USD. They exhibit _risk aversion_ : a preference for certainty over a gamble with the same expected value. This preference cannot be explained by expected value maximization.

The resolution, proposed by Daniel Bernoulli as far back as 1738, is to maximize expected _utility_ rather than expected _value_. The key insight: the utility of money is not the same as the amount of money. An additional dollar matters more to a poor person than to a rich person. Utility is a function of wealth, and that function may be concave — each additional dollar adds less utility than the previous dollar.


#### Definition: Expected Utility

Let a lottery be a probability distribution over outcomes. If the outcomes are x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n with probabilities p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n (where the p_i sum to 1), and if u(\cdot) is a utility function mapping outcomes to real numbers, then the **expected utility** of the lottery is:

EU = \sum_{i=1}^{n} p_i \cdot u(x_i)

In plain language: compute the utility of each possible outcome, multiply by its probability, and sum. The rational agent chooses the option with the highest expected utility.

The crucial step is that we evaluate _utility_ , not _money_. If the utility function is concave (utility grows but at a decreasing rate as wealth increases), then the expected utility of a gamble is less than the utility of its expected value — which means a concave-utility agent is risk averse.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: Expected Utility Theory — The Benchmark
blocks.src:
### 2.2 Risk Aversion, Risk Neutrality, and Risk Seeking

The shape of the utility function determines an agent's attitude toward risk. This is one of the most powerful ideas in decision theory, and it will reappear in Chapter 3 when prospect theory modifies the framework.

**Risk aversion** occurs when the utility function is concave — the curve bends downward (each additional dollar adds less to utility than the previous one). A risk-averse agent prefers the expected value of a gamble as a certain amount over the gamble itself.

Formally: an agent with utility function u(\\cdot) is risk averse if for any lottery L,

u(E[L]) > E[u(L)]

where E[L] is the expected value of the lottery and E[u(L)] is the expected utility of the lottery.

**Risk neutrality** occurs when the utility function is linear — each additional dollar adds the same amount to utility. A risk-neutral agent is indifferent between a gamble and its expected value as a certain amount.

**Risk seeking** occurs when the utility function is convex — each additional dollar adds _more_ to utility than the previous one. A risk-seeking agent prefers a gamble to its expected value as a certain amount.


#### Definition: Certainty Equivalent and Risk Premium

The **certainty equivalent** of a lottery is the certain amount of money that makes an agent exactly indifferent between accepting that amount and playing the lottery. Denote it CE.

The **risk premium** is the difference between the expected value of the lottery and the certainty equivalent:

RP = E[L] - CE

For a risk-averse agent, CE<E[L]CE < E[L]CE<E[L], so RP>0RP > 0RP>0. The risk premium represents how much an agent is willing to pay to eliminate risk — it is the economic foundation of insurance markets.

**Example.** Suppose an agent's utility function is u(w) = \sqrt{w} (the square root function, which is concave). The agent faces a gamble: 100 USD with probability 0.5 and 0 USD with probability 0.5.

Expected value: E[L] = 0.5 \times 100 + 0.5 \times 0 = 50 USD

Expected utility: E[u(L)] = 0.5 \times \sqrt{100} + 0.5 \times \sqrt{0} = 0.5 \times 10 + 0.5 \times 0 = 5

Certainty equivalent: We need u(CE) = 5, so \sqrt{CE} = 5, which gives CE = 25 USD.

Risk premium: RP = 50 - 25 = 25 USD.

This agent would pay up to 25 USD to avoid the gamble — that is, they would be willing to accept 25 USD with certainty rather than play the 50/50 gamble for 100 USD or 0 USD, even though the gamble's expected value is 50 USD.


#### Common Misconception

**Misconception:** Risk aversion means refusing all gambles — a risk-averse person would never voluntarily take a chance on an uncertain outcome.

**Reality:** Risk aversion means preferring a certain outcome over a gamble with the same _expected value_ , not refusing every gamble. A risk-averse person will refuse a fair gamble — but may happily accept a gamble where the expected gain exceeds their risk premium. A risk-averse person might even buy lottery tickets if the ticket price is cheap enough relative to the (tiny) probability of a very large prize. Risk aversion is about the shape of the utility function at a given wealth level, not an absolute disposition to avoid all uncertainty.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: Expected Utility Theory — The Benchmark
blocks.src:
### 2.3 The Axioms of Expected Utility Theory

Von Neumann and Morgenstern's achievement was to show that if a rational agent's preferences satisfy a small number of axioms, those preferences can be represented by an expected utility function. The axioms are not just technical formalities — each embodies a substantive claim about what rational choice requires.

**Axiom 1: Completeness.** For any two lotteries A and B, the agent either prefers A to B, prefers B to A, or is indifferent between them. Preferences are well-defined over all possible options.

**Axiom 2: Transitivity.** If the agent prefers A to B and B to C, then the agent prefers A to C. Preferences are internally consistent.

**Axiom 3: Continuity.** For any three lotteries A, B, C where A is preferred to B and B is preferred to C, there exists a probability p such that the agent is indifferent between B and the lottery that gives A with probability p and C with probability 1-p. This rules out "lexicographic" preferences where one consideration completely dominates all others.

**Axiom 4: Independence.** If the agent prefers lottery A to lottery B, then for any lottery C and any probability p in (0, 1), the agent prefers the mixture that gives A with probability p and C with probability (1-p) to the mixture that gives B with probability p and C with probability (1-p).

The independence axiom is the most important and the most violated. It says: mixing two lotteries with a common third lottery should not reverse the preference between the original two. If you prefer vanilla to chocolate ice cream, you should still prefer a 50% chance of vanilla (with 50% chance of strawberry) to a 50% chance of chocolate (with 50% chance of strawberry). The Allais paradox from Chapter 1 is precisely a violation of this axiom.

**What's at stake with the independence axiom.** Of the four axioms, independence is the one behavioral economics has spent the most energy interrogating — and for good reason. Completeness, transitivity, and continuity describe structural requirements on preference that most people satisfy in practice. Independence is different: it is the axiom that prospect theory (Chapter 3) is specifically designed to relax. The violations are systematic, predictable, and large. When people reverse their preference between two lotteries simply because both are mixed with the same third option at the same probability, they violate independence — not through confusion, but because the move from certainty to near-certainty feels qualitatively different from an equivalent shift between two uncertain options. This "certainty effect" is the heart of why expected utility theory fails as a descriptive account of risky choice. Keep the independence axiom in mind throughout the next several chapters: every time you see framing, reference points, or the shape of the probability weighting function doing work, you are seeing independence fail in action.


#### Definition: The Independence Axiom

If A \succ B (A is preferred to B), then for any lottery C and any p \in (0,1):

pA + (1-p)C \succ pB + (1-p)C

In plain language: a preference between two options should not be reversed simply by mixing both options with the same third option at the same probability.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: Expected Utility Theory — The Benchmark
blocks.src:
#### Common Misconception

**Misconception:** Expected utility theory implies that rational people are selfish and only care about money.

**Reality:** Expected utility theory says nothing about what people value — it specifies only how preferences over risky outcomes should be _structured_ to be internally consistent. A person who deeply cares about others' welfare, about fairness, or about non-monetary goals can be a fully rational expected utility maximizer; their utility function simply includes those values. EU theory is a theory of _consistency under uncertainty_ , not a theory of _selfishness_. When behavioral economics later shows that people care about fairness (Chapter 10) or social norms (Chapter 11), this is not evidence against rational choice as such — it is evidence that the common simplifying assumption that utility equals personal wealth is wrong. The axioms and the assumption that utility = money are entirely separate claims.


### 2.4 The Von Neumann–Morgenstern Representation Theorem

The four axioms together have a powerful implication: if your preferences satisfy all four, they can be represented by an expected utility function. That is, there exists a utility function u(\cdot) such that lottery A is preferred to lottery B if and only if the expected utility of A exceeds the expected utility of B.

This theorem matters for two reasons. First, it provides a _justification_ for expected utility maximization: if you accept the four axioms as requirements of rational choice, you are committed to expected utility maximization. Second, it provides a _test_ : if you find yourself violating expected utility predictions, you are violating at least one of the axioms, which might not be something you endorse on reflection.

The utility function in this framework is unique up to positive linear transformations — multiplying all utilities by a positive constant or adding a constant does not change any choices. What matters is the _shape_ of the utility function, not its scale.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: Expected Utility Theory — The Benchmark
blocks.src:
### 2.5 Applying Expected Utility: Insurance and Gambles

Expected utility theory generates clean predictions for classic economic problems.

**Insurance.** A homeowner faces a 1% probability of a 200,000 USD fire (destroying their home) and a 99% probability of no loss. Expected loss = 0.01 \times 200,000 = 2,000 USD. An actuarially fair insurance premium would charge exactly 2,000 USD for full coverage.

Would a rational, risk-averse homeowner buy this insurance? Yes, and they would even be willing to pay somewhat above 2,000 USD — their risk premium. The exact amount depends on the concavity of their utility function. Very risk-averse homeowners will pay well above 2,000 USD for certainty; near-risk-neutral homeowners will barely exceed 2,000 USD.

The prediction that risk-averse people buy actuarially fair insurance is a success of expected utility theory. Insurance markets exist precisely because expected utility predicts a demand for them.

**Gambling.** The same framework predicts that a risk-averse agent would never take a fair gamble (one with an expected value of zero). Yet gambling is enormously popular. Expected utility theory can accommodate this with a convex region of the utility function at relevant wealth levels — but this requires the utility function to flip from concave to convex, which seems arbitrary.

Prospect theory, developed in Chapter 3, offers a more satisfying explanation: people gamble not because their utility function over wealth is convex, but because they systematically overweight small probabilities of large wins.


#### Thread B — Rational vs. Human Agent

**Thread B snapshot:** The rational agent's choice architecture under uncertainty is now clear. Given a utility function and a set of lotteries, the rational agent computes expected utilities and picks the maximum. There is no role for how the gamble is described, who proposed it, whether it involves a loss relative to some reference point, or whether the probability is precisely known or merely estimated. All of that is invisible to the standard model. Chapters 3 through 6 will show that all of these "invisible" factors dominate real human choices.


### 2.6 Expected Utility and Intertemporal Choice

Expected utility theory has a natural extension to choices involving time. If outcomes arrive at different dates, the rational agent discounts future outcomes — places less utility weight on them — at a constant rate. This gives the _exponential discounting_ model, which we will treat in detail in Chapter 8.

For now, the key point: under exponential discounting, the rational agent has _time-consistent_ preferences. Their ranking of two future options does not change simply because time passes and the options get closer. If they prefer receiving 110 USD next year to 100 USD this year, they will still prefer 110 USD in a year from now to 100 USD immediately, even when "a year from now" becomes "next year" and "this year" becomes "now."

Time consistency is to intertemporal choice what the independence axiom is to risky choice: an elegantly simple requirement that real humans systematically violate.


### 2.7 Exercises

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: Expected Utility Theory — The Benchmark
blocks.src:
#### Concept Check

**Q1.** Why does the expected value maximization approach fail to explain risk aversion? How does expected utility theory resolve this problem?

**Answer:** Expected value maximization says you should always prefer the option with the highest probability-weighted monetary payoff. This cannot explain risk aversion because a risk-averse person prefers a certain 50 USD to a fair gamble averaging 50 USD — but both have the same expected value. Expected utility theory resolves this by introducing a utility function that maps money to subjective value. If the utility function is concave (diminishing marginal utility), then the utility of receiving 50 USD for certain exceeds the expected utility of the gamble, even though the expected monetary values are equal. Risk aversion emerges naturally from concave utility.

**Q2.** An agent has utility function u(w) = \ln(w) (natural log). Calculate the expected utility and certainty equivalent for the gamble: 400 USD with probability 0.5 and 100 USD with probability 0.5.

**Answer:** Expected utility:

E[u] = 0.5 \times \ln(400) + 0.5 \times \ln(100) = 0.5 \times 5.991 + 0.5 \times 4.605 = 2.996 + 2.303 = 5.299

To find the certainty equivalent, solve \ln(CE) = 5.299:

CE = e^{5.299} \approx 200 \text{ USD}

Note that the expected monetary value of the gamble is 0.5 \times 400 + 0.5 \times 100 = 250 USD. The certainty equivalent (200 USD) is below the expected value (250 USD), confirming this agent is risk averse. The risk premium is 250 - 200 = 50 USD — this agent would pay up to 50 USD to convert the gamble into its expected value.

**Q3.** State the independence axiom in plain English. Why is it considered a basic requirement of rational choice?

**Answer:** The independence axiom says: if you prefer option A to option B, then you should still prefer A to B when both are mixed with the same third option at the same probability. The rationale is that the "common part" (the third option that appears identically in both mixtures) should be irrelevant to the choice — what matters is the part that differs between the two options. If adding identical components to both sides of a preference could reverse it, your preferences would be sensitive to irrelevant information — which seems irrational. The axiom is also the mathematical foundation of the expected utility representation: without it, preferences cannot generally be represented by an expected utility function.

**Q4.** Distinguish between risk aversion, risk neutrality, and risk seeking in terms of the shape of the utility function. For each, state whether the certainty equivalent is above, equal to, or below the expected value of a gamble.

**Answer:**

* _Risk aversion_ : concave utility function (each additional dollar adds less to utility). Certainty equivalent is _below_ the expected value. The agent pays a positive risk premium to eliminate risk.
* _Risk neutrality_ : linear utility function (each additional dollar adds the same amount to utility). Certainty equivalent _equals_ the expected value. The agent is indifferent between a gamble and its expected value.
* _Risk seeking_ : convex utility function (each additional dollar adds more to utility than the previous one). Certainty equivalent is _above_ the expected value. The agent requires a premium to give up a gamble in exchange for certainty.

**Q5.** Which of the four expected utility axioms does the Allais paradox violate, and why?

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: Expected Utility Theory — The Benchmark
blocks.src: **Answer:** The Allais paradox violates the **independence axiom**. Recall that the most common pattern of choices (A over B in Problem 1, D over C in Problem 2) can be shown to imply a logical inconsistency when the independence axiom is applied. Specifically: if A is preferred to B, then mixing both with the same lottery at the same probability should preserve the preference. Problems 1 and 2 in the Allais paradox are exactly such a mixture — Problem 2 is constructed from Problem 1 by mixing each option with a fixed probability of 0 USD. The reversal of preference from C (A's mixture) to D (B's mixture) violates the axiom. People switch because the move from 100% certainty to 89% certainty feels much larger than an equivalent shift from 11% to 10%, revealing a "certainty effect" that is formally inconsistent with the independence axiom.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: Expected Utility Theory — The Benchmark
blocks.src:
#### Application Problems

**Q1.** A farmer faces a 10% probability of a drought that would reduce crop revenue from 80,000 USD to 20,000 USD. A crop insurance policy costs 6,000 USD and guarantees 80,000 USD revenue regardless of drought. The farmer's utility function is u(w) = \sqrt{w}. Should the rational farmer buy the insurance?

Hint

Compute the expected utility without insurance and compare it to the utility of the certain outcome with insurance. The farmer buys insurance if and only if the utility of (revenue minus premium) exceeds the expected utility of the uninsured gamble.

**Answer:** Without insurance:

E[u] = 0.9 \times \sqrt{80{,}000} + 0.1 \times \sqrt{20{,}000} = 0.9 \times 282.84 + 0.1 \times 141.42 = 254.56 + 14.14 = 268.70

With insurance: revenue is 80,000 USD - 6,000 USD = 74,000 USD with certainty.

u(74{,}000) = \sqrt{74{,}000} = 272.03

Since 272.03 > 268.70, the farmer with this utility function prefers to buy the insurance. Note: the expected value without insurance is 0.9 \times 80,000 + 0.1 \times 20,000 = 74,000 USD — exactly the same as the insured outcome. But the farmer pays 6,000 USD above the actuarially fair premium (0.1 \times 60,000 = 6,000 USD, so this insurance is actually actuarially fair). Because the utility function is concave, any actuarially fair insurance will be worth buying for a risk-averse agent.

**Q2.** An investor has wealth 100,000 USD and is offered an investment that pays 200,000 USD with probability 0.4 and 40,000 USD with probability 0.6 (the investment replaces their wealth, not adds to it). Their utility function is u(w) = \ln(w). (a) Should they invest? (b) What is their certainty equivalent for the investment?

Hint

Compare the expected utility of the investment to the utility of keeping 100,000 USD. For the certainty equivalent, find the certain wealth level that produces the same expected utility as the investment.

**Answer:** (a) Expected utility of investment:

E[u] = 0.4 \times \ln(200{,}000) + 0.6 \times \ln(40{,}000) = 0.4 \times 12.206 + 0.6 \times 10.597 = 4.882 + 6.358 = 11.240

Utility of keeping 100,000 USD:

u(100{,}000) = \ln(100{,}000) = 11.513

Since 11.513 > 11.240, the investor should NOT invest.

(b) Certainty equivalent: solve \ln(CE) = 11.240:

CE = e^{11.240} \approx 75{,}786 \text{ USD}

The certainty equivalent (75,786 USD) is well below the expected value of the investment (0.4 \times 200,000 + 0.6 \times 40,000 = 80,000 + 24,000 = 104,000 USD). The risk premium is approximately 104,000 - 75,786 = 28,214 USD. This investor is quite risk averse.

**Q3.** The independence axiom seems compelling when stated abstractly. But here is a challenge: Suppose you are choosing between two medical treatments. Treatment A: 80% chance of full recovery, 20% chance of remaining ill. Treatment B: 70% chance of full recovery, 30% chance of remaining ill. You prefer A. Now suppose a new treatment C (experimental) is mixed in: with 50% probability, you get the treatment you chose (A or B), and with 50% probability, you get C (a 90% chance of full recovery). The mixed lotteries are: Mixed A = 50% chance of A outcomes + 50% chance of C outcomes. Mixed B = 50% chance of B outcomes + 50% chance of C outcomes. Does the independence axiom require you to prefer Mixed A to Mixed B? Does this seem reasonable to you?

Hint

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: Expected Utility Theory — The Benchmark
blocks.src:
Work out the final probabilities in Mixed A and Mixed B. Then ask: is the independence axiom's requirement that you prefer Mixed A to Mixed B actually sensible given the final probability distributions?

**Answer:** Mixed A: 50% of the time you get A's outcomes (80% recovery, 20% ill); 50% of the time you get C (90% recovery). Final probability of recovery: 0.5 \times 0.8 + 0.5 \times 0.9 = 0.40 + 0.45 = 0.85.

Mixed B: 50% of the time you get B's outcomes (70% recovery, 30% ill); 50% of the time you get C (90% recovery). Final probability of recovery: 0.5 \times 0.7 + 0.5 \times 0.9 = 0.35 + 0.45 = 0.80.

Yes, the independence axiom requires preferring Mixed A (85% recovery) to Mixed B (80% recovery), since the difference between A and B is maintained proportionally when both are mixed with C at 50%. This seems quite reasonable — the 5-percentage-point advantage of A over B is maintained as a 5-percentage-point advantage of Mixed A over Mixed B. The independence axiom is more compelling in this health example than in the Allais paradox's financial example, which suggests that the certainty effect that drives Allais violations may be specific to the feeling of "100% certainty" rather than a general failure of independence.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: Expected Utility Theory — The Benchmark
blocks.src:
#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** Expected utility theory treats the utility function as capturing everything that matters about an outcome — once you know the utility of each outcome and its probability, you know everything needed for a rational choice. But outcomes are described in many ways in real life. Does the framing of an outcome (how it is described) affect its "utility"? What would expected utility theory say, and is that reasonable?

**Discussion:** Expected utility theory says no — the utility of an outcome is determined entirely by the outcome itself, not how it is described. If you receive 100 USD, the utility is u(100 USD) regardless of whether the 100 USD is described as "winning 100 USD" or "recovering 100 USD that you had lent" or "avoiding a loss of 100 USD." This is the foundation of what behavioral economics calls the "consequentialism" assumption: only consequences matter, not the path that leads to them or how they are framed. This seems normatively plausible — a rational person should care about what they actually end up with, not linguistic packaging. But Chapter 3 and Chapter 4 will show that people's choices are dramatically affected by framing, in ways they often regret on reflection. Behavioral economics takes framing effects seriously as empirical phenomena. The deeper question is whether framing effects always represent irrationality or whether descriptions sometimes convey genuinely different information about the social or normative context of a decision.

**Q2.** The risk premium represents how much an agent is willing to pay to eliminate uncertainty. Is the risk premium a measure of irrationality? Under what circumstances would a very high risk premium be rational, and under what circumstances might a very low risk premium (near-risk neutrality) be irrational?

**Discussion:** The risk premium is not a measure of irrationality — it is an expression of the curvature of a person's utility function and their underlying preferences. Very high risk premia (very risk-averse behavior) are rational whenever the worst outcomes are catastrophic relative to a person's resources — a family with a 200,000 USD house and 50,000 USD in savings may rationally be extremely risk averse about home fires because the downside (homelessness, debt) is genuinely catastrophic. Near-zero risk premia (near-risk neutrality) can also be rational for large, diversified institutions that pool many independent risks — an insurance company with a million policies should be nearly risk neutral toward any individual policy. The irrational case for very low risk premia in individuals would be if a person is acting as though they are an insurance company when they are actually a single household — ignoring the potentially catastrophic downside of rare events. Behavioral economics will add: people also exhibit risk-seeking behavior over _losses_ relative to a reference point, which looks like low risk aversion but is driven by prospect theory's asymmetric value function rather than a high risk tolerance in the standard sense.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: Expected Utility Theory — The Benchmark
blocks.src:
### Chapter Summary

Expected utility theory formalizes what it means to choose rationally under uncertainty. The rational agent maximizes the probability-weighted sum of utilities over possible outcomes, where the utility function captures both the value of outcomes and the agent's attitude toward risk.

Three features of this framework are worth internalizing deeply. First, risk aversion is not the same as irrationality — it follows naturally from concave utility and explains the existence of insurance markets. Second, the independence axiom is the axiom that does the most work and is most easily violated — it will be our diagnostic tool throughout the book for identifying non-expected-utility behavior. Third, the expected utility framework is _consequentialist_ : only the probability distribution over final outcomes matters, not how those outcomes are described, labeled, or presented.

Chapter 3 will take these features and systematically dismantle and rebuild them. Prospect theory retains the framework of evaluating probability-weighted outcomes, but replaces the standard utility function with a reference-dependent value function and the standard probability weights with a probability weighting function. The result is a richer theory that explains the Allais paradox, predicts risk-seeking over losses, and accounts for the asymmetric psychology of gains and losses.

The saving-for-retirement thread (Thread A) makes a quiet appearance in this chapter's foundation: the rational saver uses exponential discounting, a form of consistent intertemporal utility maximization, to determine the optimal savings rate. That rate exists, it is calculable, and a rational person would achieve it. In Chapter 8, we will see why almost no one does.

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: Prospect Theory — The Behavioral Alternative
blocks.src:
Here is a puzzle. You have just learned that you received a 500 USD bonus this month that you did not expect. You feel good. A colleague in the same situation, who expected a 1,000 USD bonus, received only 500 USD — the same 500 USD, the same bank balance — but they feel bad. Same outcome, completely different emotional experience.

Now a second puzzle. Your local grocery store raises the price of orange juice by 0.50 USD. You barely notice. A hospital raises its surgery fees by 50 USD. You are outraged. Both are fifty-cent increases per dollar-spent — but they feel entirely different, and neither feels like a simple 0.50 USD loss.

Standard expected utility theory has no vocabulary for either of these phenomena. In expected utility theory, what matters is your final wealth — not where you started, not what you expected, not how the change is described. Prospect theory, developed through decades of psychological research and formalized by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, provides that vocabulary. It is the central theoretical achievement of behavioral economics.


### 3.1 The Core Idea: Reference Points Change Everything

The key departure of prospect theory from expected utility theory is simple to state: people evaluate outcomes not in absolute terms but _relative to a reference point_. A gain is good; a loss is bad. And the reference point — what counts as zero — is not fixed at zero wealth or any other objective level. It is psychological, shifting with circumstances, expectations, and framing.

Consider the grocery store puzzle again. The shopper buying juice might have a reference point of "the price I paid last week." Any increase feels like a loss. The hospital patient's reference point is the same: what they expected to pay. But hospital fees feel like losses from a much more emotionally significant reference point — health, control, vulnerability — which is why a proportionally identical increase triggers far more outrage.

This insight — that outcomes are evaluated as gains or losses relative to a reference point — is the foundation of prospect theory. Everything else follows from it.


#### Definition: Reference Point

A **reference point** is the psychological baseline from which outcomes are evaluated. Outcomes above the reference point are perceived as _gains_ ; outcomes below it are perceived as _losses_. The reference point is not fixed at zero wealth — it shifts with context, expectations, recent experience, and framing.

In plain language: the reference point is your "status quo" — the outcome you expected or were used to. Winning 500 USD when you expected 500 USD feels like nothing gained. Winning 500 USD when you expected 0 USD feels like a windfall. Same outcome, different reference point, completely different experience.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: Prospect Theory — The Behavioral Alternative
blocks.src:
### 3.2 The Value Function

Prospect theory replaces the expected utility function with a _value function_ defined over gains and losses relative to the reference point. The value function has three characteristic features.

**Feature 1: Reference dependence.** The domain of the value function is gains and losses, not final wealth levels. Denote a gain of amount x (above the reference point) as +x and a loss of amount x below the reference point as -x.

**Feature 2: Loss aversion.** Losses hurt more than equivalent gains please. The value function is steeper in the loss domain than in the gain domain. Formally:

|v(-x)| > |v(+x)| \quad \text{for all } x > 0

The psychological research suggests the loss aversion coefficient (how much more losses hurt relative to gains) is approximately 2 to 2.5 — a loss of 100 USD produces roughly twice as much negative affect as a gain of 100 USD produces positive affect. This ratio is not universal — it varies by person, domain, and stakes — but the qualitative pattern (losses loom larger) is one of the most robustly replicated findings in behavioral economics.

**Feature 3: Diminishing sensitivity.** The value function is concave in the gain domain and convex in the loss domain. Going from 0 to 100 USD feels larger than going from 100 USD to 200 USD. Going from 0 to -100 USD feels worse than going from -100 USD to -200 USD. Each additional unit of gain or loss has less psychological impact than the one before it.


#### Definition: Diminishing Sensitivity

**Diminishing sensitivity** means that the psychological impact of a change diminishes with distance from the reference point. This applies symmetrically to gains (concave value function) and losses (convex value function). Adding 100 USD to a gain of 10 USD feels large; adding 100 USD to a gain of 10,000 USD feels small. The same unit change matters less the further you are from zero.

In plain language: your first 100 USD gain matters a lot; your 101st 100 USD gain matters much less. And your first 100 USD loss is deeply distressing; your 100th additional 100 USD loss, while terrible, is slightly less distressing than the first.

The combination of loss aversion and diminishing sensitivity produces a characteristic shape: the value function is steeper on the loss side, and both sides curve away from a linear function — concave (curving down) for gains and convex (curving up) for losses. Imagine a letter S stretched asymmetrically, with the loss side being steeper and longer than the gain side.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: Prospect Theory — The Behavioral Alternative
blocks.src:
#### Common Misconception

**Misconception:** Loss aversion and risk aversion are the same thing — both describe a general tendency to avoid unfavorable outcomes.

**Reality:** They are related but mechanistically distinct. _Risk aversion_ (from standard expected utility) says you prefer certainty over a fair gamble — it follows from a concave utility function over final wealth. _Loss aversion_ says you are more sensitive to losses than gains of the same magnitude — it follows from the kink at the reference point in the value function. Crucially, you can be loss averse and risk seeking simultaneously: prospect theory predicts risk seeking _over losses_ (the convex loss domain means a gamble is preferred to a certain loss of the same expected value) while remaining risk averse _over gains_. Risk aversion is about the utility function's curvature; loss aversion is about asymmetry across the reference point. This distinction matters for prediction: standard risk aversion would predict symmetric cautious behavior, while loss aversion predicts the fourfold pattern of risk attitudes that standard theory cannot explain.


### 3.3 The Probability Weighting Function

The second major departure of prospect theory from expected utility theory involves how probabilities are treated. Standard expected utility theory uses objective probabilities directly — a 10% chance gets a weight of 0.10. Prospect theory replaces this with a _probability weighting function_ \pi(p) that transforms objective probabilities before they enter the evaluation.

The probability weighting function has two characteristic features:

**Feature 1: Overweighting of small probabilities.** Events with small objective probabilities receive decision weights larger than their objective probability. \pi(0.01) > 0.01. People treat a 1% chance almost like a 5% or 10% chance — they overreact to small but nonzero probabilities.

**Feature 2: Underweighting of large probabilities.** Events with large (but not certain) probabilities receive decision weights smaller than their objective probability. \pi(0.95) < 0.95. People discount high-probability events — a 95% chance feels like less than 95%.

**Feature 3: Certainty and impossibility are treated as qualitatively special.** \pi(0) = 0 and \pi(1) = 1 — impossible events are given zero weight and certain events are given weight 1. But there is a discontinuity: moving from 0% to 1% (from impossible to possible) produces a much larger change in decision weight than moving from 1% to 2%, and moving from 99% to 100% (from probable to certain) produces a much larger change than moving from 98% to 99%.


#### Definition: Probability Weighting Function

The **probability weighting function** \pi(p) maps objective probabilities p \in [0, 1] to decision weights \pi(p). In prospect theory, the expected value calculation uses decision weights rather than objective probabilities:

V(L) = \sum_{i} \pi(p_i) \cdot v(x_i - r)

where v is the value function, r is the reference point, and x_i - r is the gain or loss associated with outcome i.

In plain language: instead of weighting each outcome by its probability, we weight it by a transformed probability. Small probabilities get inflated; large (non-certain) probabilities get deflated; certainty remains certainty.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: Prospect Theory — The Behavioral Alternative
blocks.src:
### 3.4 The Fourfold Pattern of Risk Attitudes

The combination of the reference-dependent value function and the probability weighting function produces prospect theory's most distinctive empirical prediction: the fourfold pattern of risk attitudes.

Domain | Probability | Risk Attitude | Example  
---|---|---|---  
Gains | High | Risk averse | Accept certain 950 USD over 95% chance of 1,000 USD  
Gains | Low | Risk seeking | Buy a lottery ticket (small prob, large prize)  
Losses | High | Risk seeking | Prefer 95% chance of -1,000 USD to certain -950 USD  
Losses | Low | Risk averse | Buy insurance against rare disasters  
  
The top-left and bottom-right cells explain behavior that standard expected utility theory cannot: buying insurance (risk aversion over low-probability losses) and buying lottery tickets (risk seeking over low-probability gains) simultaneously. Both follow from overweighting small probabilities combined with the reference-dependent value function.

The bottom-left cell — risk seeking over high-probability losses — explains a pervasive phenomenon in everyday life: people who are in financial trouble continue to take gambles to "get back to even," even when the odds are bad. This is sometimes called the "break-even effect." It also explains the behavior of investors who hold losing stocks too long (hoping to get back to the reference point) rather than cutting their losses.


#### Thread B — Rational vs. Human Agent

**Standard theory predicts:** Given a utility function defined over final wealth and a set of lotteries, the rational agent computes expected utilities and maximizes. The reference point at which they started has no effect on choices. A person with 110,000 USD who gained 10,000 USD should make the same choices as a person with 110,000 USD who lost 10,000 USD — both have the same wealth and the same expected utility function.

**Humans do:** Make completely different choices depending on whether they are in the "gain frame" (up from their reference point) or "loss frame" (down from their reference point). A person who is up from their reference point tends toward risk aversion; a person who is down tends toward risk seeking. The two people with the same 110,000 USD but different histories make systematically different decisions — exactly as prospect theory predicts and exactly opposite to standard theory's prediction.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: Prospect Theory — The Behavioral Alternative
blocks.src:
### 3.5 The Editing Phase

Prospect theory describes decision-making as a two-stage process. Before evaluating lotteries, people first _edit_ them — simplify and restructure them using a set of cognitive operations. Key editing operations include:

**Coding:** Outcomes are coded as gains or losses relative to a reference point established during editing.

**Combination:** Probabilities associated with identical outcomes are combined. A gamble offering 100 USD with probability 0.3 and 100 USD with probability 0.2 is simplified to 100 USD with probability 0.5.

**Segregation:** Components that are risk-free are segregated from risky components. A gamble offering 100 USD with certainty plus a 50/50 chance of winning or losing 50 USD is broken into a certain gain of 100 USD and a zero-expected-value gamble.

**Cancellation:** Components shared by all options under consideration are discarded. If all options in a choice set include a 30% chance of 200 USD, that component is ignored (cancelled) when comparing the options. This operation is responsible for many framing effects — which common component is highlighted affects which components are cancelled.

The editing phase is important because it is where framing effects enter. Two logically equivalent presentations of the same lottery may be edited differently, leading to different choices — even though the final distributions are identical. Chapter 4 explores framing effects in depth.


### 3.6 Explaining the Allais Paradox

We can now revisit the Allais paradox from Chapter 1 and show how prospect theory explains it.

Recall the choices. In Problem 1: A (certain 1M USD) is typically preferred to B (89% chance of 1M USD, 10% chance of 5M USD, 1% chance of 0 USD). In Problem 2: D (10% chance of 5M USD, 90% chance of 0 USD) is typically preferred to C (11% chance of 1M USD, 89% chance of 0 USD).

The reference point for all options is 0 USD (no winnings). All outcomes are gains. The probability weighting function explains the pattern:

In Problem 1, the certainty of Option A (\pi(1) = 1) contrasts sharply with the near-certainty of the best outcome in Option B (\pi(0.89) is less than 0.89 due to underweighting). The certain 1M USD is disproportionately attractive because certainty has a qualitative premium — it eliminates all anxiety about the bad outcome.

In Problem 2, both options have low probabilities. The difference between \pi(0.11) and \pi(0.10) is small (neither receives much overweighting premium for being "small"). What dominates is the much larger prize in Option D (5M USD vs. 1M USD). So D is chosen.

The mathematical structure: suppose \pi(1) = 1, \pi(0.89) = 0.71, \pi(0.11) = 0.14, \pi(0.10) = 0.13, and \pi(0.01) = 0.05 (illustrative values consistent with probability weighting research). Then:

For Problem 1:

V(A) = 1 \times v(1M) = v(1M) V(B) = 0.71 \times v(1M) + 0.13 \times v(5M) + 0.05 \times v(0)

If v(5M) < 5 \times v(1M) (diminishing sensitivity), then V(A) > V(B) is plausible — the certainty premium for A outweighs the small gain from B's higher prize.

For Problem 2, the low-probability structure reduces both weights proportionally, and the prize difference dominates: D's high prize wins.

This is not a trick — prospect theory, with reasonable parameter values, generates exactly the Allais pattern that expected utility theory cannot explain.


### 3.7 Exercises

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: Prospect Theory — The Behavioral Alternative
blocks.src:
#### Concept Check

**Q1.** What is the reference point in prospect theory? Give two examples of how the same outcome can be perceived differently depending on the reference point.

**Answer:** The reference point is the psychological baseline from which outcomes are evaluated. Outcomes above the reference point are gains; below are losses.

Example 1: A worker receives a 2% salary increase. If their reference point is "last year's salary," this is a gain. If their reference point is "the 5% increase their colleague got" or "the inflation rate of 4%," this same 2% increase is perceived as a loss. Same objective outcome, different emotional valence.

Example 2: An investor buys a stock at 100 USD. If the stock falls to 80 USD and later rises to 90 USD, the investor with a reference point of 100 USD (purchase price) feels a loss of 10 USD. But an investor who just learned about the stock at 80 USD (when recommending it to a friend) uses 80 USD as the reference point and feels a gain of 10 USD. Same position (90 USD/share), completely different psychological experience.

**Q2.** Describe the three key features of the value function in prospect theory. How does each feature differ from the standard utility function of expected utility theory?

**Answer:**

  1. _Reference dependence_ : The value function is defined over gains and losses relative to a reference point, not over final wealth levels. Standard utility is defined over total wealth — a person with 110,000 USD always has the same utility regardless of how they got there.

  2. _Loss aversion_ : The value function is steeper in the loss domain than in the gain domain — losses are felt more acutely than equivalent gains. Standard utility has no such asymmetry; an increase in wealth of xxx USD from any level increases utility by the same amount as a decrease of xxx USD decreases it (for a symmetric utility function).

  3. _Diminishing sensitivity_ : The value function is concave for gains (each additional dollar of gain feels smaller) and convex for losses (each additional dollar of loss feels smaller too). Standard utility theory has concavity throughout (for a risk-averse agent), producing risk aversion over both gains and losses.

**Q3.** What is the fourfold pattern of risk attitudes predicted by prospect theory? Give a real-world example of each quadrant.

**Answer:**

Domain | Probability | Attitude | Real-world example  
---|---|---|---  
Gains | High | Risk averse | Accepting a certain job offer over a riskier but higher-paying one  
Gains | Low | Risk seeking | Buying lottery tickets despite negative expected value  
Losses | High | Risk seeking | Delaying debt repayment hoping for a windfall rather than accepting the certain loss  
Losses | Low | Risk averse | Buying insurance against rare events (floods, identity theft)  
  
Each quadrant is explained by the combination of the value function shape and the probability weighting function: certainty effects (qualitative premium on certainty) drive the high-probability cells; probability overweighting drives the low-probability cells.

**Q4.** In standard expected utility theory, a person's choices should depend only on their final wealth level, not on how they got there. How does prospect theory's concept of reference dependence challenge this?

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: Prospect Theory — The Behavioral Alternative
blocks.src:
